questions.q: Which of the following is the unit of molarity?
questions.explanation: Molarity is moles of solute per litre of solution, so its unit is mol per litre.

questions.q: Which of the following is the SI base unit of mass?
questions.explanation: The kilogram is the SI base unit of mass; the litre is not an SI base unit and metre and kelvin measure length and temperature.

questions.q: What is the mass of one atom of carbon-12 in grams? (NA = 6.022 × 10^23 per mol)
What is the molecular mass of glucose, C6H12O6? (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
What is the percentage of nitrogen by mass in urea, CO(NH2)2? (C = 12, O = 16, N = 14, H = 1)
In the reaction 4NH3 + 5O2 → 4NO + 6H2O, what mass of NO is formed from 17 g of NH3 with excess oxygen? (N = 14, O = 16, H = 1)
questions.explanation: 17 g of NH3 is 1 mol, and 4 mol NH3 gives 4 mol NO, so 1 mol NO = 30 g.

questions.q: 100 mL of 0.2 M HCl is mixed with 100 mL of 0.4 M HCl. What is the molarity of the resulting solution?
questions.explanation: Total moles = 0.02 + 0.04 = 0.06 mol in 0.2 L, giving 0.3 M.

questions.q: Define mole fraction and calculate the mole fraction of ethanol in a mixture of 1 mol ethanol and 4 mol water.
questions.answer: Mole fraction of a component is its moles divided by the total moles of all components; for ethanol it is 1/(1 + 4) = 0.2.
keyPoints: Mole fraction = moles of component / total moles
questions.explanation: Mole fractions of all components add up to 1, so water is 0.8.

questions.q: A hydrocarbon contains 85.7% carbon and 14.3% hydrogen by mass and has a molar mass of 42 g/mol. Find its molecular formula.
questions.explanation: The molecular formula is the empirical formula multiplied by the ratio of molar mass to empirical formula mass.

questions.q: Who discovered the neutron?
questions.explanation: Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932 by bombarding beryllium with alpha particles.

questions.q: The plum pudding model of the atom was proposed by
questions.explanation: Thomson proposed that electrons are embedded in a positively charged sphere, like plums in a pudding.

questions.q: How many electrons are present in the 3d subshell of an iron atom (Z = 26) in the ground state?
questions.explanation: The configuration of iron is [Ar] 3d6 4s2, so there are six 3d electrons.

questions.q: What is the maximum number of electrons that can be accommodated in a 4f subshell?
questions.explanation: An f subshell has 7 orbitals, each holding 2 electrons, so 14 in total.

questions.q: According to Bohr's model, the angular momentum of an electron in a stationary orbit is
questions.explanation: Bohr's quantisation condition is mvr = nh/2π, with n = 1, 2, 3 and so on.

questions.q: What is the frequency of light of wavelength 600 nm? (c = 3 × 10^8 m/s)
What is the maximum number of electrons in an atom that can have the quantum numbers n = 3 and ml = +1?
questions.explanation: ml = +1 occurs in the 3p subshell and the 3d subshell, giving two orbitals, which hold 4 electrons.

questions.q: Distinguish between an orbit and an orbital.
questions.answer: An orbit is a fixed circular path of an electron around the nucleus in Bohr's model; an orbital is a three-dimensional region around the nucleus where the probability of finding an electron is high, described by a wave function.
keyPoints: Orbital: region of probability from quantum mechanics
An orbital holds at most two electrons
questions.explanation: The orbital concept follows from the uncertainty principle, which does not allow definite paths.

questions.q: A photon has an energy of 4.97 × 10^-19 J. Calculate its wavelength. (h = 6.626 × 10^-34 J s, c = 3 × 10^8 m/s)
questions.explanation: The wavelength lies at the violet end of the visible spectrum.

questions.q: How many elements are there in the second period of the periodic table?
questions.explanation: The second period runs from lithium to neon, which is 8 elements.

questions.q: The lanthanoids belong to which block?
questions.explanation: In lanthanoids the 4f subshell is being filled, so they are f-block elements.

questions.q: Which of the alkali metals Li, Na, K and Cs has the highest first ionisation enthalpy?
questions.explanation: Ionisation enthalpy decreases down a group as atomic size increases, so lithium has the highest.

questions.q: Which halogen is a liquid at room temperature?
questions.explanation: Fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a liquid and iodine is a solid at room temperature.

questions.q: Which of the following ions is isoelectronic with argon?
questions.explanation: Argon has 18 electrons, and Ca2+ (20 - 2 = 18) has the same number.

questions.q: Which of the following oxides is the most acidic?
questions.explanation: Acidic character of oxides increases across a period, and Cl2O7 is a strongly acidic oxide of a non-metal.

questions.q: Atomic size decreases across a period from left to right mainly because
options: the effective nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same shell
electrons are removed from the atoms
questions.explanation: Each step adds one proton and one electron in the same shell, so the pull on outer electrons strengthens.

questions.q: What are isoelectronic species? Give two examples.
questions.answer: Atoms or ions with the same number of electrons; for example Na+ and Mg2+ (and F- and Ne), which all have 10 electrons.
keyPoints: Examples: O2-, F-, Ne, Na+, Mg2+
questions.explanation: In an isoelectronic series, radius decreases as nuclear charge increases.

questions.q: The electron gain enthalpy of fluorine is less negative than that of chlorine. Explain.
questions.answer: The fluorine atom is very small, so the added electron enters a compact 2p subshell where strong electron-electron repulsion reduces the energy released.
keyPoints: Fluorine has a very small 2p subshell
Chlorine's larger 3p subshell accommodates the electron more easily
questions.explanation: Hence chlorine has the most negative electron gain enthalpy of all the elements.

questions.q: An electrovalent (ionic) bond is usually formed between
questions.explanation: Metals of low ionisation enthalpy lose electrons to non-metals of high electron gain enthalpy, forming ions.

questions.q: Which of the following diatomic molecules contains a triple bond?
questions.explanation: N2 has the structure N≡N, with one sigma and two pi bonds.

questions.q: What is the shape of the sulphur dioxide molecule, SO2?
questions.explanation: Sulphur has two bond pairs and one lone pair (sp2), giving a bent molecule.

questions.q: Which of the hydrogen halides HF, HCl, HBr and HI has the highest boiling point?
questions.explanation: HF forms strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds, which raise its boiling point above the others.

questions.q: What is the hybridisation of sulphur in SF6?
questions.explanation: Six bond pairs around sulphur require six hybrid orbitals, giving an octahedral sp3d2 arrangement.

questions.q: How many lone pairs are present on the nitrogen atom in ammonia, NH3?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen has five valence electrons; three form N-H bonds and the other two form one lone pair.

questions.q: Which pair of species has the same shape (is isostructural)?
questions.explanation: Both NH3 and H3O+ have three bond pairs and one lone pair on the central atom, so both are pyramidal.

questions.q: Define dipole moment and give its common unit.
questions.answer: Dipole moment is the product of the magnitude of the charge and the distance between the charges in a polar bond or molecule; its common unit is the debye (D).
questions.explanation: Molecules with zero net dipole moment, such as CO2, are non-polar even if their bonds are polar.

questions.q: Explain why BF3 is planar while NH3 is pyramidal.
questions.answer: Boron in BF3 has three bond pairs and no lone pair (sp2, trigonal planar), whereas nitrogen in NH3 has three bond pairs and one lone pair (sp3), which pushes the bonds into a pyramidal shape.
keyPoints: BF3: three bond pairs, no lone pair, sp2
NH3: three bond pairs plus one lone pair, sp3
Lone pair repulsion distorts NH3 from tetrahedral to pyramidal
questions.explanation: The number of lone pairs on the central atom determines the molecular shape.

questions.q: Which of the following gases is the easiest to liquefy?
questions.explanation: CO2 has strong intermolecular attractions and a high critical temperature, so it liquefies readily, unlike the very weakly attracting He, H2 and Ne.

questions.q: At 273 K and 1 atm, one mole of an ideal gas occupies approximately
questions.explanation: The molar volume at 273 K and 1 atm is 22.4 L.

questions.q: A gas at 1 atm occupies 4 L. At constant temperature it is compressed to 2 L. What is the new pressure?
questions.explanation: By Boyle's law, P2 = P1V1/V2 = 1 × 4/2 = 2 atm.

questions.q: A gas in a rigid container has a pressure of 2 atm at 300 K. What is its pressure at 450 K?
questions.explanation: At constant volume P is proportional to T, so P2 = 2 × 450/300 = 3 atm.

questions.q: In the van der Waals equation, the constant 'a' is a measure of
options: the magnitude of the attractive forces between gas molecules
the volume of one mole of molecules
the number of molecules in the gas
questions.explanation: The term a n^2/V^2 corrects for intermolecular attractions, so a larger 'a' means stronger attractions.

questions.q: At the same temperature, how many times greater is the root mean square speed of H2 molecules than that of O2 molecules?
questions.explanation: u_rms is proportional to 1/sqrt(M), so the ratio is sqrt(32/2) = 4.

questions.q: The surface tension of a liquid decreases when the temperature is raised because
options: the kinetic energy of molecules increases and the effective intermolecular attraction weakens
questions.explanation: Greater molecular motion reduces the net inward pull on surface molecules, so surface tension falls.

questions.q: State Charles's law.
questions.answer: At constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of a gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature (V/T = constant).
keyPoints: Pressure and amount of gas constant
V is directly proportional to T
questions.explanation: Extrapolating the graph of V against T gives zero volume at -273.15 °C.

questions.q: Calculate the volume occupied by 2.2 g of carbon dioxide at 300 K and 1 atm, assuming ideal behaviour. (C = 12, O = 16; R = 0.0821 L atm K^-1 mol^-1)
questions.explanation: Substituting into the ideal gas equation gives 1.23 L.

questions.q: Which thermodynamic quantity is a measure of the disorder of a system?
questions.explanation: Entropy measures the randomness or disorder of a system.

questions.q: In an exothermic reaction carried out in an open container, the temperature of the surroundings
questions.explanation: An exothermic reaction releases heat to the surroundings, so their temperature rises.

questions.q: The standard enthalpy of formation of liquid water is -286 kJ/mol. What is the enthalpy change for 2H2(g) + O2(g) → 2H2O(l)?
questions.explanation: The equation forms 2 mol of water, so ΔH = 2 × (-286) = -572 kJ.

questions.q: A system loses 50 J of heat and has 30 J of work done on it. What is ΔU?
A gas expands from 1 L to 4 L against a constant external pressure of 2 atm. What is the work done on the gas?
questions.explanation: w = -P ΔV = -2 × (4 - 1) = -6 L atm, negative because the gas does work on the surroundings.

questions.q: A reaction has a positive ΔH and a negative ΔS. Its spontaneity is
questions.explanation: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS has a positive ΔH and a positive -TΔS, so ΔG is positive at every temperature.

questions.q: The burning of 1.0 g of a fuel in a calorimeter raises the temperature of 500 g of water by 10 K. How much heat is absorbed by the water? (specific heat of water = 4.18 J g^-1 K^-1)
What is meant by the standard enthalpy of formation of a compound?
questions.answer: It is the enthalpy change when one mole of the compound is formed from its elements in their most stable states under standard conditions (1 bar pressure, usually 298 K).
keyPoints: One mole of the compound formed
From elements in their standard states
questions.explanation: By convention the standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its standard state is zero.

questions.q: State the second law of thermodynamics in terms of entropy and use it to explain why heat flows from a hot body to a cold body.
questions.answer: The entropy of the universe increases in every spontaneous process. When heat flows from hot to cold, the entropy gained by the cold body exceeds the entropy lost by the hot body, so the total entropy rises.
keyPoints: Total entropy of universe increases in spontaneous change
Entropy change q/T is larger for the cold body
questions.explanation: Since the same heat q is divided by a lower temperature for the cold body, its entropy gain is greater.

questions.q: At chemical equilibrium
options: the concentrations of reactants and products are equal
the rates of the forward and backward reactions are equal
all the reactants have been used up
questions.explanation: Equilibrium is dynamic: both reactions continue at equal rates, so concentrations stay constant.

questions.q: Which of the following is a strong acid?
questions.explanation: HCl ionises almost completely in water, whereas the other three are weak acids.

questions.q: What is the pH of 0.05 M sulphuric acid, assuming that both hydrogen ions ionise completely?
An aqueous solution of which salt is acidic?
questions.explanation: NH4+ is the conjugate acid of a weak base and hydrolyses to give H3O+, while Cl- does not hydrolyse.

questions.q: What is the conjugate acid of ammonia, NH3?
questions.explanation: NH3 accepts a proton to form NH4+, its conjugate acid.

questions.q: The molar solubility of Ca(OH)2 in water is 1 × 10^-3 M. What is its solubility product, Ksp?
For PCl5(g) ⇌ PCl3(g) + Cl2(g), what happens to the amount of PCl5 at equilibrium if extra Cl2 is added at constant temperature?
questions.explanation: Adding a product shifts the equilibrium backward, forming more PCl5.

questions.q: State Le Chatelier's principle.
questions.answer: If a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change in concentration, pressure or temperature, the equilibrium shifts in the direction that tends to counteract the change.
keyPoints: Applies to a system at equilibrium
Change in concentration, pressure or temperature
Equilibrium shifts to oppose the change
questions.explanation: It allows us to predict how conditions change the yield, for example in the Haber process.

questions.q: Calculate the pH of the solution obtained by mixing 100 mL of 0.2 M HCl with 100 mL of 0.1 M NaOH.
keyPoints: Excess H+ = 0.01 mol in 0.2 L = 0.05 M
questions.explanation: The strong base neutralises half the acid, leaving 0.05 M H+.

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of hydrogen in most of its compounds with non-metals?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen is +1 in compounds with non-metals and -1 only in metal hydrides.

questions.q: In any redox reaction, the number of electrons lost by the reducing agent is
options: equal to the number of electrons gained by the oxidising agent
questions.explanation: Electrons are conserved: those released in oxidation are taken up in reduction.

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of phosphorus in H3PO4?
What is the oxidation number of carbon in methanol, CH3OH?
Which of the following is the strongest oxidising agent?
questions.explanation: Oxidising power of the halogens decreases down the group, and fluorine is the strongest.

questions.q: Which of the following is a redox reaction?
questions.explanation: Magnesium changes from 0 to +2 and oxygen from 0 to -2, while the others involve no change of oxidation numbers.

questions.q: Which element is oxidised in Cu + 2AgNO3 → Cu(NO3)2 + 2Ag?
questions.explanation: Copper changes from 0 to +2, so it loses electrons and is oxidised.

questions.q: What is a half-reaction? Write the oxidation half-reaction for zinc metal turning into zinc ions.
questions.answer: A half-reaction shows either the oxidation or the reduction part of a redox reaction separately, with the electrons; for zinc: Zn → Zn2+ + 2e-.
keyPoints: Shows only the oxidation or only the reduction
questions.explanation: Adding the oxidation and reduction half-reactions gives the overall redox equation.

questions.q: In Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2, identify the oxidising agent and the reducing agent with the changes in oxidation number.
questions.answer: Fe2O3 is the oxidising agent (Fe goes from +3 to 0); CO is the reducing agent (C goes from +2 to +4).
keyPoints: Fe2O3 is oxidising agent, CO reducing agent
questions.explanation: This is the key reaction in the blast furnace extraction of iron.

questions.q: Which of the following is the lightest metal?
questions.explanation: Lithium has a density of about 0.53 g/cm3, the lowest of all metals.

questions.q: Alkali metals are strong reducing agents because
options: they readily lose their single valence electron
they have very small atomic sizes
questions.explanation: Their low ionisation enthalpies make them lose electrons easily, which reduces other substances.

questions.q: What flame colour does a potassium compound give?
questions.explanation: Potassium gives a lilac flame; sodium is golden yellow, calcium brick red and lithium crimson.

questions.q: What is the chemical formula of gypsum?
questions.explanation: Gypsum is calcium sulphate dihydrate, CaSO4·2H2O.

questions.q: Hydrogen peroxide is stored in dark or plastic bottles because it
options: decomposes in light to give water and oxygen
reacts with glass to form hydrogen
questions.explanation: 2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2 is accelerated by light, and traces of alkali from glass also speed it up.

questions.q: Which of the following is an electron-deficient hydride?
questions.explanation: B2H6 has too few electrons to form normal two-centre bonds for all its atoms, whereas CH4 is electron-precise and NH3 and H2O are electron-rich.

questions.q: What is plaster of Paris? Write the equation for its setting with water.
questions.answer: Plaster of Paris is calcium sulphate hemihydrate, CaSO4·1/2 H2O. On mixing with water it sets to gypsum: CaSO4·1/2 H2O + 1 1/2 H2O → CaSO4·2H2O.
keyPoints: Made by heating gypsum at about 393 K
questions.explanation: It is used for plastering fractured bones and for making moulds and statues.

questions.q: Lithium chloride is soluble in organic solvents but sodium chloride is not. Explain.
questions.answer: The small Li+ ion has high polarising power, so LiCl has considerable covalent character according to Fajans' rules and dissolves in less polar solvents; NaCl is almost purely ionic.
keyPoints: Li+ is very small with high charge density
questions.explanation: Covalent compounds dissolve in organic solvents, while ionic ones do not.

questions.q: The chief ore of aluminium is
questions.explanation: Bauxite, Al2O3·2H2O, is the main ore of aluminium; cryolite is used only to lower the melting point in electrolysis.

questions.q: Which allotrope of carbon consists of football-shaped molecules?
questions.explanation: Buckminsterfullerene, C60, has 60 carbon atoms arranged in a cage like a football.

questions.q: On heating in the borax bead test, borax first gives
questions.explanation: Na2B4O7 → 2NaBO2 + B2O3, forming a transparent glassy bead that is used for detecting metals.

questions.q: How many oxygen atoms is each silicon atom bonded to in the structure of silicon dioxide?
questions.explanation: In SiO2 each silicon is tetrahedrally bonded to four oxygen atoms in a giant network.

questions.q: Water gas is a mixture of
questions.explanation: Water gas, made by passing steam over red-hot coke, consists of carbon monoxide and hydrogen.

questions.q: CO2 is a gas while SiO2 is a hard solid with a very high melting point because
options: silicon is more electronegative than carbon
CO2 consists of discrete molecules with weak forces between them, whereas SiO2 is a giant covalent network
questions.explanation: Melting SiO2 requires breaking strong covalent bonds throughout the network, but CO2 only needs weak intermolecular forces overcome.

questions.q: What are silicones? Mention two uses.
questions.answer: Silicones are organosilicon polymers with a repeating -R2Si-O- chain. They are used as lubricants and sealants, in water-proofing materials and in medical implants.
keyPoints: Polymers with Si-O-Si backbone and organic groups
questions.explanation: They are made by hydrolysis and condensation of alkyl chlorosilanes.

questions.q: Show with equations that aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric.
questions.answer: With acid: Al(OH)3 + 3HCl → AlCl3 + 3H2O. With alkali: Al(OH)3 + NaOH → Na[Al(OH)4]. It behaves as a base with acids and as an acid with bases.
keyPoints: Reacts with HCl to give salt and water
Reacts with NaOH to give sodium tetrahydroxoaluminate
questions.explanation: A substance reacting with both acids and bases is called amphoteric.

questions.q: Which of the following is an alkene?
questions.explanation: C2H4 (ethene) contains a carbon-carbon double bond, so it is an alkene.

questions.q: A carbon atom forming four single bonds is
questions.explanation: Four sigma bonds around carbon need four equivalent hybrid orbitals, so it is sp3.

questions.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH3CH2COOH?
questions.explanation: Three carbons including the carboxyl carbon give propanoic acid.

questions.q: The reaction CH3Cl + OH- → CH3OH + Cl- is an example of
questions.explanation: The nucleophile OH- replaces the chloride leaving group on carbon.

questions.q: Which of the following shows geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism?
questions.explanation: In but-2-ene each double-bonded carbon has two different groups (H and CH3), so cis and trans forms exist.

questions.q: Ethanol and dimethyl ether, both C2H6O, are examples of
questions.explanation: One has an -OH group (alcohol) and the other an ether group, so they are functional isomers.

questions.q: Distinguish between saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons with one example each.
questions.answer: Saturated hydrocarbons contain only single C-C bonds (for example ethane), whereas unsaturated hydrocarbons contain at least one double or triple carbon-carbon bond (for example ethene or ethyne).
keyPoints: Saturated: only single bonds, e.g. ethane
Unsaturated: C=C or C≡C present, e.g. ethene
questions.explanation: Unsaturated compounds undergo addition reactions, unlike saturated ones.

questions.q: Why are the two carbon-oxygen bonds in the acetate ion, CH3COO-, equal in length?
questions.answer: The negative charge is delocalised over both oxygen atoms through resonance, so each C-O bond has partial double-bond character and the bonds are identical.
keyPoints: Bond length intermediate between C-O and C=O
questions.explanation: The real structure is a resonance hybrid, not either single drawn structure.

questions.q: Which of the following alkanes is a gas at room temperature?
questions.explanation: The first four straight-chain alkanes (C1 to C4) are gases at room temperature.

questions.q: What is the general formula of the alkyne series?
questions.explanation: Alkynes with one triple bond have the formula CnH2n-2.

questions.q: Hydration of ethyne with dilute H2SO4 and HgSO4 gives
questions.explanation: The initial vinyl alcohol is unstable and rearranges (tautomerises) to ethanal.

questions.q: Benzene reacts with chloromethane in the presence of anhydrous AlCl3 to give
questions.explanation: This Friedel-Crafts alkylation puts a methyl group on the ring, forming methylbenzene (toluene).

questions.q: A mixture of CH3Cl and C2H5Cl is heated with sodium in dry ether. How many different alkanes can be formed?
questions.explanation: The Wurtz reaction can couple like or unlike groups, giving ethane (CH3-CH3), propane (CH3-C2H5) and butane (C2H5-C2H5).

questions.q: Benzene reacts with chlorine in bright sunlight (UV) without a catalyst to give mainly
questions.explanation: Under UV light chlorine adds across the ring by a free radical mechanism, giving 1,2,3,4,5,6-hexachlorocyclohexane.

questions.q: Write the equation for the reaction of ethene with bromine and state what is observed.
questions.answer: CH2=CH2 + Br2 → CH2Br-CH2Br (1,2-dibromoethane). The reddish-brown colour of bromine is discharged.
keyPoints: Electrophilic addition across the double bond
questions.explanation: This decolourisation is used as a test for unsaturation.

questions.q: Arrange n-pentane, isopentane and neopentane in increasing order of boiling point and explain.
questions.answer: Neopentane < isopentane < n-pentane. Branching makes the molecule more compact, which reduces surface area and so van der Waals forces.
keyPoints: Weaker dispersion forces mean lower boiling point
questions.explanation: The straight-chain isomer has the largest contact area between molecules and therefore the highest boiling point.
